232263466_b36db484.text: The forebrain noradrenergic input is from a small bilateral collection of neurons called the locus coeruleus (LC), where the cells begin rostrally at the level of the inferior colliculus adjacent to the cerebral aqueduct and end caudally near the lateral wall of the fourth ventricle (German et al., 1988) ; on axial brain slices, the anatomical landmarks are 1 mm under the fourth ventricle, 3 mm from the midline, and centred 14-21 mm above the ponto-medullary junction (Fernandes et al., 2012) (Fig. 1)

232263466_1a98ef2e.text: .Other conventional ways to identify noradrenaline producing neurons in the LC is by immunohistochemistry directed at tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the enzyme that converts L-tyrosine to L-DOPA, or against dopamine betahydroxylase, which converts dopamine to noradrenaline. (Iversen et al., 1983) It is widely considered that the two markers are expressed by identical neuronal populations (Chan-Palay et al., 1989) representing the noradrenergic neuronal population of LC which constitutes more than 95% of neurons in the LC in controls. (Baker et al., 2004)(Oh et al., 2019)

232263466_959af3b0.text: Within the LC there is heterogeneity in both the population of the residing medium-sized neurons and neuronal numbers across the rostro-caudal gradient. The majority of medium-sized LC noradrenergic neurons are large multipolar cells (35-45 mm in diameter), with plump cell bodies and short dendrites; in the caudal LC and subcoeruleus, where the density of medium sized neurons is lower, the larger medium sized neurons are interspersed with smaller fusiform noradrenergic neurons (15 mm in diameter) with triangular cell bodies and two tufts of long dendrites. 19
